results.q: How did the workers end up opening the wrong flange at PEMEX?
results.text:
They opened the wrong flange because the marking system did not clearly point them to Blind 407, so they used the wrong visual cue. The Repcon boilermakers said they were looking for orange-and-blue blind tags or unlocked red flange-locking devices instead of the blind list or drawing. [pemex-012]

At the Blind 407 location, there were two similar piping segments only 5 feet apart. The intended ARU6 piping had been depressurized, purged, and isolated, but the nearby ARU7 piping was still active and contained hydrogen sulfide. The workers said they did not see the Blind 407 tag, which was fastened to the railing above the blind. Instead, they saw a flange-locking device on the ARU7 flange and believed that was the work location. [pemex-012]

The CSB said PEMEX Deer Park did not have a clearly defined system to identify equipment for opening during Run-and-Maintain work. The blind tags were not consistently placed directly on the flange, and the flange-locking devices were never meant to identify equipment for opening. That combination led the workers to pick the active line by mistake. [pemex-019][pemex-020][pemex-025]

results.text:

results.q: What caused the furnace explosion at Shell Polymers Monaca?
results.text:
The furnace explosion at Shell Polymers Monaca was caused by the inadvertent simultaneous opening of both motor-operated valves used to isolate Furnace 5. That opened a path for cracked gas to backflow into the furnace firebox, where the existing flame ignited it and caused the explosion. [monaca-037][monaca-015]

Several factors contributed. A PACO engineer with limited process knowledge was assigned to manipulate the valves. Shell relied on administrative controls that were ineffective for preventing the backflow hazard. The safety system’s HMI also made the valves hard to distinguish because it put three similar valves on one diagram without clear labels. [monaca-037][monaca-002]

In the incident itself, cracked gas accumulated in the firebox for about 2.5 minutes before igniting. The blast damaged Furnace 5, caused a fire, led to the evacuation of 15 employees, and Shell estimated about $95 million in property damage. [monaca-016][monaca-017]

results.q: What caused the furnace explosion at Shell Polymers Monaca?
results.text:
The Shell Polymers Monaca furnace exploded because both motor-operated isolation valves were opened at the same time by mistake. That created a path for cracked gas to flow back into Furnace 5’s firebox, where lit pilots ignited it. [monaca-037][monaca-015][monaca-016]

The CSB said several things contributed to that mistake. Shell assigned a process control engineer with limited process knowledge to operate the valves, relied on ineffective administrative controls instead of engineered protection, and used an HMI that put the valves on one screen with unclear labels, which made confusion more likely. [monaca-037][monaca-002]

In the event itself, cracked gas backed into the firebox for about 2.5 minutes and then ignited, causing the explosion and a fire. Shell estimated about 515 pounds of non-combusted cracked gas and about 4,600 pounds of combustion products were released, and the explosion caused about $95 million in property damage. [monaca-016][monaca-017]

results.q: What did the CSB recommend to Shell Polymers?
results.text:
The CSB recommended two actions to Shell Polymers Monaca.

First, Shell should review the ethane cracking unit process hazard analysis to find process deviations that are handled only with administrative controls, and then put in an inherently safer design or an engineered control for any scenario that could lead to a fatality, serious injury, or major property damage. [monaca-038]

Second, Shell should, using licensor input and good industry practices, implement and maintain an engineered control that prevents backflow of cracked gas into a furnace in all modes of furnace operation. [monaca-038]

The report also says Shell had already taken corrective actions after the incident, so the CSB did not make additional recommendations on some of the specific valve-control issues. Instead, it urged Shell to make sure those new controls are fully implemented and consistently followed on all furnaces at the facility. It also urged periodic cleaning of the furnace coke traps according to Linde’s guidance. [monaca-038]

results.q: What mechanical integrity problems did the CSB find in the 2023 Honeywell reboiler explosion?
results.text:
The CSB found that Honeywell’s mechanical integrity system did not manage the reboiler’s known thinning problem to safe closure. In October 2021, Honeywell’s reliability group inspected the reboiler and found the shell was approaching Tmin, meaning it needed replacement. The site also documented signs of wall loss and a low UT reading, but there was no evidence of a proper fitness-for-service evaluation, and the “fit for service” note was not supported. [geismar-028]

The CSB said Honeywell then failed to do the basic MI follow-through. It did not create the required SAP deficiency notification, did not create the DMAPS action item, did not set up a notification for the next inspection, and did not keep the problem visible to operations, maintenance, and management. [geismar-034][geismar-031]

The report also says the site had a long history of reboiler shell corrosion and repeated shell replacements, but Honeywell did not preserve key thickness data from earlier shells and did not fully investigate why corrosion behavior changed in earlier failures. [geismar-024][geismar-025][geismar-028]

In short, the MI problems were failure to document the deficiency, failure to communicate it, failure to schedule and track corrective action, and failure to replace the shell before the 2023 rupture. [geismar-034][geismar-069]

results.q: What mechanical integrity problems did the CSB find in the 2023 Honeywell reboiler explosion?
results.text:
The CSB found that Honeywell’s mechanical integrity system failed to keep the reboiler from running to catastrophic failure. After an October 2021 inspection, Honeywell knew the shell was approaching minimum thickness and needed replacement, but it did not create the required deficiency notification in SAP, did not create a DMAPS action item, and did not create a next-inspection notification. As a result, the problem was not tracked to closure and no later inspection was done before the January 2023 rupture. [geismar-030][geismar-031][geismar-034]

The CSB also found that Honeywell did not adequately document or preserve key inspection information. The company could not produce documentation for a claimed UT inspection in October 2021, and it did not preserve the thickness data for earlier shell failures, which limited later review of the corrosion history. [geismar-028][geismar-025]

On the physical side, the failed shell had thinned severely from HF corrosion. After the accident, metallurgical examination found some spots as thin as 0.030 inches, far below Tmin. [geismar-028] The earlier shell history also showed recurring thinning, leaks, and a prior case where the shell had dropped below Tmin and had to be removed from service. [geismar-024][geismar-026]

In short: the MI problems were missed escalation, poor tracking, poor documentation, and failure to replace or re-inspect a shell the site already knew was nearing failure. [geismar-030][geismar-034]

results.q: Why was Reactor 6's relief system inadequate at Givaudan?
results.text:
Reactor 6’s relief system was inadequate because it was the wrong size for the runaway sugar decomposition reaction that happened that day. The CSB said the system did function as designed, but it was undersized, so the gas and pressure could not be relieved fast enough and the reactor kept building pressure until it ruptured. The existing emergency pressure relief system would have needed to be about four times larger to prevent the rupture; the CSB also said a 4-inch rupture disc alone should have provided enough relief capacity. [givaudan-060][givaudan-035]

The report also says the relief system design for Reactor 6 was based on Reactor 2, but the facility did not have documentation showing the design basis for Reactor 2’s relief system. In other words, the team did not have a clear documented basis showing that the chosen relief arrangement could handle this reaction scenario. [givaudan-033][givaudan-063]

results.q: Why was Reactor 6's relief system inadequate at Givaudan?
results.text:
Reactor 6’s relief system was inadequate because it was too small for the runaway sugar decomposition reaction that happened that day. The CSB said the relief system did function as designed, but it could not relieve the gas and pressure fast enough, so the pressure kept rising until the reactor ruptured. [givaudan-035][givaudan-060]

The system on Reactor 6 used a 4-inch rupture disc and a 4M6 pressure relief valve in series. The CSB’s modeling found that a much larger relief system would have been needed to prevent rupture: either a pressure relief valve with at least 16.74 square inches of relief area, or a 4-inch rupture disc alone instead of the valve-plus-disc arrangement. [givaudan-033][givaudan-035]

The report also says the design team did not have clear documentation of the earlier relief-system changes on other reactors, and that this lack of records helped lead to an undersized design for Reactor 6. [givaudan-042][givaudan-062]

results.q: What was the means-of-egress problem in the Wacker incident?
results.text:
The means-of-egress problem was that the fifth-floor platform where the workers were exposed had only a single way out. Wacker had designed the structure as an “unoccupiable equipment platform,” so it treated the access stair as enough under the building code. But Wacker’s own Process Hazard Analysis had already identified the risk of having only one exit and recommended adding a second means of egress, such as a ladder with an enclosed cage on the opposite end of the structure, if the route to the stairs was blocked. That recommendation was not implemented before the incident. [wacker-002][wacker-027][wacker-028]

The CSB said this mattered because the hydrogen chloride release happened while seven workers were on that platform, and the limited egress could have prevented workers from getting out safely. [wacker-002][wacker-033]

results.q: What was the means-of-egress problem in the Wacker incident?
results.text:
The means-of-egress problem was that the fifth-floor platform had only one staircase, so when the hydrogen chloride cloud made that path unusable, the workers had no second way out. [wacker-001][wacker-013]

Wacker had already identified this in its process hazard analysis three months earlier. The analysis asked what would happen if there were an HCl leak and workers had to move through the cloud to reach the stairs, and it recommended installing a ladder or other alternate exit on the opposite side of the structure. That second exit was not installed before the incident. [wacker-027]

The CSB said the limited egress contributed to the severity of the event. It also said the building codes and standards then in place did not provide sufficient means of egress for elevated work platforms used to access hazardous materials equipment. [wacker-034][wacker-031]

results.q: Which incidents involved problems with pressure relief systems?
results.text:
Based on the six reports, the incidents with pressure relief system problems were:

- **Dow Louisiana Operations**: the product cooler’s pressure relief system was part of the event. The report says the rupture disc and PRV combination existed, the discharge piping lost its inert atmosphere, and the pressure relief piping and vent routing contributed to the explosion severity. The report also says the pressure relief system was undersized for the reaction and that venting to the reflux drum made the consequences worse. [dow-006][dow-026][dow-030][dow-012]
- **Givaudan Sense Colour**: Reactor 6 had an emergency pressure relief system, but it was **undersized** for the runaway reaction. The report says the relief system functioned, but it could not relieve enough gas and pressure to prevent the reactor rupture. [givaudan-033][givaudan-035][givaudan-061]

The other reports retrieved here do **not** show pressure relief system problems as the main issue:
- **PEMEX Deer Park**: the passages retrieved are about equipment identification and blind removal, not pressure relief. [pemex-017][pemex-045]
- **Shell Polymers Monaca**: the passages retrieved are about MOVs, alarms, and bypassing, not pressure relief systems. [monaca-019][monaca-026][monaca-029]
- **Honeywell Geismar**: the passages retrieved are about mechanical integrity, gaskets, reboilers, and trapped HF, not pressure relief systems. [geismar-031][geismar-055][geismar-071]

results.text:
The incidents with pressure relief system problems were Dow Louisiana Operations and Givaudan Sense Colour. [dow-006][dow-012][dow-031][givaudan-033][givaudan-035]

At Dow, the pressure relief system for the product cooler was part of the problem. The product cooler’s relief piping was routed to the reflux drum, and the CSB said Dow did not adequately assess the risk of venting to a vessel full of reactive ethylene oxide. When ethylene oxide entered the relief piping, it ignited, propagated to the PRV, and then into the reflux drum, which overpressured and failed catastrophically. [dow-006][dow-012][dow-031]

At Givaudan, the emergency pressure relief system did function, but it was undersized for the runaway reaction in Reactor 6. The CSB said the relief system, a rupture disc and pressure relief valve in series, could not adequately relieve the gases and pressure generated, so the reactor ruptured. [givaudan-033][givaudan-034][givaudan-035]

The other four reports I checked did not show a pressure relief system as a central issue in the passages returned. They focused instead on line opening errors at PEMEX, furnace valve control at Monaca, HF releases and maintenance practices at Honeywell Geismar, and a torquing-related nozzle fracture at Wacker. results.q: What do the PEMEX and Wacker incidents have in common?
results.text:
They have a few things in common.

Both incidents involved maintenance work that went wrong on operating equipment. At PEMEX, workers opened the wrong piping and released hydrogen sulfide; at Wacker, a contractor over-torqued bolts on live equipment and released hydrogen chloride [pemex-048][wacker-034].

Both incidents were made worse because the companies did not adequately control the work before it started. PEMEX did not have an effective way to clearly identify the correct equipment and did not adequately control the hazards of opening piping in an active unit [pemex-017][pemex-002]. Wacker did not have written procedures for the torquing task and did not treat the work as needing hazardous-energy controls or a risk analysis [wacker-001][wacker-033].

Both incidents also involved contract workers and problems with safe work permitting. PEMEX’s permit process was broad and unclear, and Repcon workers were moved from a shutdown turnaround unit to an active unit without enough warning about the hazards [pemex-002][pemex-046]. Wacker’s permitting process did not identify the interaction between the torquing work and the insulation work happening nearby [wacker-019][wacker-033].

Finally, in both cases, the releases hurt people who were nearby and not part of the task. PEMEX caused two fatalities and injuries to other contractors [pemex-016]. Wacker caused one fatality and serious injuries after workers tried to escape the cloud and fell from the structure [wacker-001][wacker-033].

results.q: What do the PEMEX and Wacker incidents have in common?
results.text:
They have the same basic pattern: both incidents happened during maintenance on operating equipment, and both were made worse by weak work planning and weak control of the hazard.

In the PEMEX incident, workers opened the wrong piping during a maintenance job, releasing toxic hydrogen sulfide. The CSB said PEMEX did not have an effective way to clearly identify the correct equipment to open, and its permit system did not control the hazard or protect nearby contractors in the adjacent turnaround unit. [pemex-001][pemex-048]

In the Wacker incident, a contractor over-torqued bolts on a live HCl piping flange during maintenance, which cracked the equipment and released gaseous hydrogen chloride. The CSB said Wacker lacked written procedures for the torquing task and did not treat the work as hazardous energy control work. [wacker-001][wacker-034]

A second thing they share is that other workers nearby were put at risk because the companies did not properly evaluate simultaneous or adjacent work. At PEMEX, dozens of contractors were exposed to the hydrogen sulfide release. [pemex-002] At Wacker, another contractor crew was working on the same structure and was unnecessarily exposed to the HCl release. [wacker-002][wacker-033]

So, in plain terms: both were maintenance jobs on hazardous process equipment, both involved wrong or uncontrolled work on live systems, and both showed failures in identification, permitting, and coordination with other work nearby. [pemex-046][wacker-033]

results.q: Which of the reports made recommendations to OSHA?
results.text:
The reports made recommendations to OSHA in three of the six incidents: Shell Polymers Monaca, Honeywell Geismar, and Wacker Polysilicon. [monaca-038][geismar-073][wacker-036]

- **Shell Polymers Monaca**: the report’s recommendations were to Shell, not OSHA. I did not find an OSHA recommendation there. [monaca-038]
- **Honeywell Geismar**: the report reiterated a recommendation to OSHA to amend the PSM standard so it explicitly requires management of organizational and personnel change. [geismar-072][geismar-043]
- **Wacker Polysilicon**: the report made recommendations to OSHA on simultaneous operations, including requiring coordination of SIMOPs and developing guidance on SIMOPs. [wacker-036][wacker-037]
- **Givaudan Sense Colour**: the report reiterated a recommendation to OSHA to broaden PSM coverage of reactive hazards. [givaudan-066][givaudan-005]

So, the reports with OSHA recommendations were **Givaudan Sense Colour, Honeywell Geismar, and Wacker Polysilicon**. [givaudan-066][geismar-072][wacker-036]

results.q: What did the CSB conclude about the Evergreen Packaging incident?
results.text:
The CSB concluded that the Evergreen Packaging incident was the Dow Louisiana Operations explosions report. It found that metal debris from portable work lights left in a reflux drum degraded and moved downstream, where it punctured a rupture disc and let ethylene oxide enter pressure relief piping that contained air. The ethylene oxide ignited, the flame and combustion products propagated to a reflux drum filled with ethylene oxide, and the drum failed catastrophically from the pressure rise caused by decomposition. [dow-032]

The CSB also said Dow’s inadequate vessel-closure practices allowed the work lights to be left in the drum, its failure to maintain an inert atmosphere in the pressure relief piping let the ethylene oxide ignite, and the design that vented relief back into the reflux drum made the consequences much worse. [dow-032][dow-003]
